implementation_notes: Calling lazy on any Enumerable returns an Enumerator::Lazy whose chain is not evaluated until something forces it (each, to_a, first), so select, map, reject and filter_map become composable stages and the enumerator plays the pipe's role; plain Enumerable methods are eager and allocate one array per stage, which is exactly the cost the pattern avoids. This is the idiomatic in-process realisation and it replaces the classic filter classes entirely. When the stages are separate executables, Open3.pipeline composes them with real OS pipes instead.
pitfalls: lazy must be called before the chain: on an eager Enumerable every stage materialises a new array, so the pipeline costs more than the monolith it replaced.
A lazy enumerator is single-pass per force: each call re-reads and re-runs the source, repeating side effects and I/O.
filter_map hides a two-in-one stage (select plus map); keep drop-versus-transform decisions explicit when the pipeline is part of a public contract.

variants.name: Open3 process pipeline over existing tools
variants.idiom_name: Open3.pipeline(cmd1, cmd2, .., in:, out:) with real OS pipes
variants.implementation_notes: Open3.pipeline starts a whole chain of external programs in one call, wires real pipes between them and returns the Process::Status of every stage, so existing command-line filters (grep, gzip, sort, awk) can be composed without being rewritten - the POSIX pipe-and-filter form with Ruby as the assembler. pipeline_r/pipeline_w expose the ends for streaming and pipeline_start exposes wait_thr for incremental reading. It costs process startup and text serialisation, so keep the in-process lazy chain for pure Ruby transformations.
variants.code_sketch:
require 'open3'
statuses = Open3.pipeline(
  ['cat', 'orders.txt'],
  ['grep', '-v', '^#'],
  ['sort'],
  out: 'orders.sorted'
)
raise 'pipeline failed' unless statuses.all?(&:success?)
pitfalls: A failure in a middle stage does not stop later stages automatically; without inspecting every status a truncated output looks like success.
Every stage's stdout/stderr must be consumed or redirected - an unconsumed pipe fills the OS buffer and deadlocks the chain (use pipeline_r for the reader end).
Shell-quoting and argument passing: prefer the array form (as above) over a single string, otherwise values are exposed to shell interpretation.
